abstract: Aims Heart failure (HF) is a global health challenge due to its high incidence, mortality, and socioeconomic burden. Despite medical advancements, HF prognosis remains poor, highlighting the need for enhanced understanding and treatment strategies. Serum albumin, a key circulatory protein, has gained attention as a biomarker in cardiovascular diseases. Low serum albumin levels are linked to HF incidence, progression, and prognosis, suggesting its regulatory role, though mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to elucidate the role of serum albumin in HF pathogenesis and investigate its potential therapeutic effects. Methods and results A mouse model of pressure overload-induced HF was established via transverse aortic constriction (TAC). Serum albumin levels were significantly decreased in HF mice. Administration of recombinant mouse serum albumin (rMSA) effectively restored serum albumin concentrations, improved cardiac systolic function, alleviated cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, and reduced inflammatory responses, collectively attenuating disease progression. In contrast, albumin-knockout (Alb-/-, AKO) HF mice displayed aggravated pathological manifestations compared with wild-type (WT) controls, whereas rMSA supplementation markedly ameliorated these impairments. In vitro experiments demonstrated that rMSA protected against phenylephrine (PE)-induced hypertrophy in cardiomyocytes. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, transcriptomic analyses of cardiac tissues revealed that albumin played a critical role in improving mitochondrial homeostasis. Experimental validation further demonstrated that albumin activated the PKA-LKB1-AMPK signaling axis, leading to improved mitochondrial respiratory function and oxidative phosphorylation, as well as enhanced mitochondrial quality control. These changes promoted fatty acid oxidation and optimized energy metabolism, thereby reversing the energy imbalance underlying cardiac dysfunction. Conclusion Our study suggests that serum albumin exerts a protective effect in HF by improving mitochondrial dysfunction and energy metabolism disorders, thus reversing energy imbalance and mitigating disease progression. These results support recombinant serum albumin as a promising therapeutic for HF, with its mechanism involving the critical improvement of mitochondrial homeostasis.
